newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS - CA battle lines drawn before deadline.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - CA battle lines drawn before deadline.

text.p: Austrian Creditanstalt's full-year earnings, possibly the last set of profit data before the bank loses its independence, received a muted reception on Thursday as a debate over the bank's sale reached fever pitch.
Creditanstalt reported a 20 percent rise in preliminary net profit to 2.6 billion schillings ($235 million), while its operating profit was almost flat at 6.2 billion schillings.

Chief executive Guido Schmidt-Chiari, who may have to go once the government has picked a buyer for its 70 percent voting stake in Austria's flagship bank, said the results were "quite positive", but analysts and investors took a cautious stance.

"It looks like they're squeezing all that they can out to paint a pretty picture (ahead of the sale)," said James Capel analyst Claire Fargeot, adding that the figures looked better at face value than they were fundamentally.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima is due to close the latest tender for Austria's establishment bank at 9 am (0800 GMT) on Friday and is expected to choose a buyer for the bank before or over the weekend.

The Social Democrat minister on Thursday reiterated he would not be bullied by his party's junior coalition partner, the conservative People's Party, into selling the bank to anybody but the highest bidder.

"Investment house J.P. Morgan said that the Bank Austria offer is the highest and strategically the best," he said. "And if I don't sell to the highest bidder I automatically break European Union law -- and every Austrian would also have the right to sue me."

Market leader Bank Austria has put up 16.8 billion schillings for control of its main competitor. The bank's supervisory board was meeting on Thursday to consider adjustments to its offer, but was not expected to make any changes to what is already widely billed as the winning bid.
A consortium led by Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali on Thursday raised its original 13.8 billion schillings offer for the stake, but gave no further details.

Sources close to the talks said the group had no chance of outbidding Bank Austria, the candidate of choice of the dominant Social Democrats, and that even members of the group had given up hope of winning the privatisation battle.
The sale of the state's 19.9 million voting shares in the bank has turned into an ugly political mudfight which has caused a rift in the uneasy government coalition.

The People's Party, which together with Creditanstalt's top management strongly supports EA-Generali's bid, has called for a special session of parliament on Tuesday to discuss the sale. Coalition leaders agreed to meet for an emergency session on Saturday afternoon to try to iron out their differences.
Meanwhile, Creditanstalt executives continued with their own behind-the-scenes campaign to discredit Bank Austria's bid.
Embattled chief executive Schmidt-Chiari warned investors, who have grown increasingly wary over the political uncertainty surrounding the sale, may suffer if Bank Austria got the prize.

"The precise effect on the share price cannot be estimated with certainty but, judging from other companies which have come under the control of a majority owner, the potential (for the shares) is certainly limited," he said.
Creditanstalt's shares were down about one percent on the Vienna bourse on Thursday. ($1=11.05 Schilling)
